\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The observation}
Run Pollard's rho method against $N=p\,q$ with $p=4093$ fixed and the cofactor $q$ grown
from $2^{14}$ to $2^{23}$. The measured iteration count does not grow; nor does that of
the elliptic curve method; trial division's does, dramatically, as soon as the cofactor
becomes the least prime factor. In a controlled study (fixed $p=4093$, nine independent
draws per cell, medians reported to suppress seed luck) the observed median spread over
$2^{23}$ of cofactor growth was $\times 2.16$ for the elliptic curve method and
$\times 1.40$ for rho --- flat within the intrinsic scatter of the methods themselves.
Scaling in $p$ separates them cleanly:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lccl}
\toprule
method & measured slope per $\log_2 p$ & predicted & interpretation\\
\midrule
Pollard rho & $0.45$ & $0.5$ & birthday bound $\sqrt p$\\
trial division & $1.09$ & $1$ & linear in $p$: the definition face\\
elliptic curve method & $1.13$ & sub-exponential & locally power-like, constant-advantaged\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The elliptic curve slope is misleading in isolation: the method is
constant-advantaged, needing $6\,657$ operations at $p=2^{14}$ against trial division's
$12\,142$, with its sub-exponential bending beyond the measured window.

\subsection{Two properties, not one}
The phrase ``factor-local'' conflates \emph{cofactor flatness},
$\cost(pq)=\cost(pq')$ for all cofactors, and \emph{factor boundedness},
$\cost(N)\le g(p)$. Trial division is factor bounded (by $p-1$) yet not cofactor flat;
rho is both. This separation is what gives the subject theorems rather than folklore.

\section{The cost model}

\begin{definition}
A sequence $s:\N\to\beta$ \emph{collides at time} $n$ if $s_i=s_n$ for some $i<n$. The
\emph{collision time} $T(s)$ is the least such $n$; it exists when $\beta$ is finite.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Pigeonhole ceiling]\label{lem:pigeon}
If $|\beta|=c$ then $T(s)\le c$ for every $s:\N\to\beta$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The $c+1$ values $s_0,\dots,s_c$ cannot be pairwise distinct.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:congr}
If $s_n=t_n$ for all $n$, then $T(s)=T(t)$; and if $s$ collides at $n$ but at no $m<n$,
then $T(s)=n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{cost model} is a map $\cost:\N\times\N\to\N$, where $\cost(N,p)$ is the cost of
the run modulo $N$ hunting the prime $p$. It is \emph{factor bounded} if
$\cost(N,p)\le g(p)$ for some $g$; \emph{cofactor flat} if $\cost(pq,p)=\cost(pq',p)$
for all positive $q,q'$; and \emph{modulus-determined} if $\cost(N,p)=\cost(N,p')$ for
all $p,p'$.
\end{definition}

\section{The shadow theorem}

\begin{definition}
For $f\in\Z[X]$ and a commutative ring $R$, the polynomial step is $x\mapsto f(x)$ in
$R$ and the orbit from $x_0$ is $\mathcal{O}_f(x_0)_n=f^{(n)}(x_0)$. Pollard's rho method
is $f=X^2+c$; the cubic restart variant is $f=X^3+c$; the successor map is $f=X+1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Equivariance]\label{lem:equiv}
For every ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to S$ and every $f\in\Z[X]$ we have
$\varphi(f(x))=f(\varphi(x))$, hence
$\varphi(\mathcal{O}_f(x_0)_n)=\mathcal{O}_f(\varphi(x_0))_n$ for all $n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Ring homomorphisms preserve sums, products and images of integers; induct on $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shadow theorem]\label{thm:shadow}
Let $p\mid N$, $f\in\Z[X]$, $x_0\in\Z$, and let $\pi_p:\Z/N\to\Z/p$ be reduction. Then
for every $n$,
\[
\pi_p\bigl(\mathcal{O}_f(x_0\bmod N)_n\bigr)=\mathcal{O}_f(x_0\bmod p)_n .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:equiv} to $\varphi=\pi_p$, a ring homomorphism since $p\mid N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
$T_f(p,N,x_0):=T(\pi_p\circ\mathcal{O}_f(x_0\bmod N))$ is the cost of the run modulo $N$
hunting $p$; $T_f(p,x_0):=T(\mathcal{O}_f(x_0\bmod p))$ is the intrinsic cost.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:intrinsic}
$T_f(p,N,x_0)=T_f(p,x_0)$ for every multiple $N$ of $p$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The sequences are pointwise equal by Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow}; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:congr}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cofactor flatness]\label{thm:flat}
$T_f(p,pq,x_0)=T_f(p,pq',x_0)$ for all cofactors $q,q'$. The ratio is exactly $1$; the
measured $\times1.40$ spread for rho is seed luck, not cofactor dependence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Factor boundedness]\label{thm:bound}
$T_f(p,N,x_0)\le p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The shadow takes values in $\Z/p$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pigeon}.
\end{proof}

\section{Naturality is the mechanism}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{uniform step} $M$ assigns to each commutative ring $R$ a map $M_R:R\to R$ with
$\varphi\circ M_R=M_S\circ\varphi$ for every ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to S$.
\end{definition}

Every polynomial step is uniform, as is $x\mapsto x^k$, the exponentiation step
underlying the $p-1$ method.

\begin{theorem}[Locality from naturality]\label{thm:nat}
For every uniform step $M$, every $p\mid N$ and every seed:
(i) the mod-$p$ shadow of the mod-$N$ orbit is the mod-$p$ orbit;
(ii) the cost is cofactor flat;
(iii) the cost is at most $p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) is the naturality square for $\pi_p$, iterated; (ii) follows because both sides
equal the intrinsic mod-$p$ cost; (iii) is Lemma~\ref{lem:pigeon} in $\Z/p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The $p-1$ method is cofactor flat. Writing $k(B)=\lcmop(1,\dots,B)$ for the stage-1
scalar, it fires whenever $B\ge p-1$, since the multiplicative group modulo $p$ has
order $p-1$ and $(p-1)\mid k(B)$; the least such budget is therefore at most $p-1$, and
is attained.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}
For any uniform method the shadow's collision time is at most the collision time of the
run modulo $N$: post-composition can create coincidences but never destroy them.
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}[Locality is not speed]\label{rem:speed}
The successor step $x\mapsto x+1$ in $\Z/p$ is uniform, yet its orbit visits all $p$
residues before repeating, so its collision time is exactly $p$: the bound of
Theorem~\ref{thm:bound} is sharp, and any square-root gain comes from the statistics of
the particular map, not from locality.
\end{remark}

\section{The birthday window and exact anchors}

\begin{theorem}[Birthday bound]
For $0<k\le p$,
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{i}{p}\Bigr)\;\le\;\exp\Bigl(-\frac{k(k-1)}{2p}\Bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each factor obeys $1-i/p\le e^{-i/p}$, all factors are nonnegative for $k\le p$, and
$\sum_{i<k} i=k(k-1)/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
At $p=4093$ and $k=76$ one gets $\prod_{i<76}(1-i/4093)\le 1/2$: in the uniform model
$76$ steps make a collision more likely than not, reproducing the classical constant
$1.18\sqrt{p}\approx 75.5$.
\end{corollary}

The following are exact statements about the orbit of $f(x)=x^2+1$ from $x_0=2$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:4093}
Modulo $4093$ the states $x_0,\dots,x_{69}$ are pairwise distinct and $x_{70}=x_{53}$;
the collision time is exactly $70$, within the window $2\lfloor\sqrt{4093}\rfloor=128$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:1009}
Modulo $1009$ the orbit is purely periodic from the seed: $x_{49}=x_0$ and the first
$49$ states are distinct, so the collision time is exactly $49$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
Modulo $3$ the orbit is stationary ($2^2+1\equiv 2$), so the collision time is $1$.
\end{proposition}

\section{Trial division and a rigidity theorem}

\begin{definition}
Ascending trial division inspects $2,3,\dots$ until a divisor is found; its cost is
$\td(N)=\minFac(N)-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
If $2\le d<\minFac(N)$ then $d\nmid N$: the inspected candidates genuinely fail, so
$\td(N)$ is the true count of failed tests.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[The definition face]
If $p\le q$ are primes then $\minFac(pq)=p$ and $\td(pq)=p-1$. Hence across two such
strata $\td(pq)/\td(p'q')=(p-1)/(p'-1)$ identically, matching the measured slope
$1.09$ per $\log_2 p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
For every prime $p\mid N$ we have $\td(N)\le p-1$: trial division is factor bounded.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Not cofactor flat]\label{thm:tdflat}
$\td(4093\cdot 3)=2$ while $\td(4093\cdot 4093)=4092$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity]\label{thm:rigid}
A cost model that is modulus-determined and cofactor flat is constant on composites:
$\cost(ab)=\cost(cd)$ for all positive $a,b,c,d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Modulus-determinedness permits free re-labelling of the hunted factor. By flatness with
hunted factor $a$ and cofactors $b$ and $cd$, $\cost(ab)=\cost(a(cd))$. Since
$a(cd)=(cd)a$, flatness with hunted factor $cd$ and cofactors $a$ and $1$ gives
$\cost((cd)a)=\cost(cd\cdot 1)=\cost(cd)$. Chain the equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Trial division is modulus-determined and non-constant on composites, hence cannot be
cofactor flat: Theorem~\ref{thm:tdflat} is an instance of a structural obstruction.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}
The rho cost model is not modulus-determined: it costs $1$ at $p=3$ and $70$ at
$p=4093$ --- exactly the freedom Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid} shows a nontrivial flat model
must have.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Certified separation]
With $T(1009)=49$ and $T(4093)=70$ from Propositions~\ref{prop:1009} and~\ref{prop:4093},
\[
20\cdot T(1009)\le \td(1009^2)=1008,\qquad 58\cdot T(4093)\le \td(4093^2)=4092 .
\]
The advantage grows from $\ge 20\times$ to $\ge 58\times$: two exact points of the
$0.45$-versus-$1.09$ slope separation.
\end{proposition}

\section{The elliptic curve ledger is cofactor-free}

Stage 1 forms $k(B)=\lcmop(1,\dots,B)$ and multiplies a point of a random curve by
$k(B)$ modulo $N$ with a guarded inversion. Modulo a prime $p$ the point lies in a group
of order $m$ with $|m-(p+1)|\le 2\sqrt p$ by Hasse's theorem; write
$H(p)=p+3+2\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor\ge m$.

\begin{lemma}[Firing count]\label{lem:fire}
In the cyclic model the multiplier state is a residue $a$ modulo $m$ and the scalar
\emph{fires} when $m\mid ka$. The firing set has exactly $\gcd(m,k)$ elements.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$m\mid ka$ iff $(m/\gcd(m,k))\mid a$, and there are $\gcd(m,k)$ such $a<m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:mono}
If $B\le B'$ then $k(B)\mid k(B')$, so $\gcd(m,k(B))\le\gcd(m,k(B'))$. If $m\le B$ then
$m\mid k(B)$ and $\gcd(m,k(B))=m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Cofactor-free rate]\label{thm:rate}
Let $N=pq$ with mod-$p$ group order $m$ and mod-$q$ group order $m'$. A random point is
a uniform pair in $\Z/m\times\Z/m'$; the number of joint states whose mod-$p$ coordinate
fires is $\gcd(m,k)\,m'$, so the mod-$p$ success rate is
\[
\frac{\gcd(m,k)\,m'}{m\,m'}=\frac{\gcd(m,k)}{m},
\]
a function of the factor and the bound only: the cofactor order cancels identically.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
The expected curve count is $C(m,B)=m/\gcd(m,k(B))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
If $m\le H(p)$ then $C(m,B)\le H(p)=p+3+2\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$ for every $B$ and every
cofactor; moreover $B\le B'$ implies $C(m,B')\le C(m,B)$, so the cost curve in $B$ has
no wall; and if $0<m\le H(p)\le B$ then $C(m,B)=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$C(m,B)\le m\le H(p)$; antitonicity and the wall case follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}
and $C=m/m=1$ when the scalar annihilates the group.
\end{proof}

\section{Exact two-prime outcome counts and ledger faithfulness}

Fix group orders $m_p,m_q>0$ and a scalar $k$; write $F_p=\gcd(m_p,k)$,
$F_q=\gcd(m_q,k)$. A trial is a pair $(a,b)\in\Z/m_p\times\Z/m_q$. Separate four
outcomes: \emph{dead} (both fire; the guarded inversion returns $N$),
\emph{found$_p$}, \emph{found$_q$}, and \emph{nothing}.

\begin{theorem}[Exact block counts]\label{thm:blocks}
\[
|\mathrm{dead}|=F_pF_q,\quad |\mathrm{found}_p|=F_p(m_q-F_q),\quad
|\mathrm{found}_q|=(m_p-F_p)F_q,
\]
\[
|\mathrm{nothing}|=(m_p-F_p)(m_q-F_q),
\]
and the four blocks partition all $m_pm_q$ trials.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each block is a Cartesian product of a firing or co-firing set in each coordinate; apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:fire} and the product rule. The sum factors as
$(F_p+(m_p-F_p))(F_q+(m_q-F_q))=m_pm_q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact reveal count]
The found blocks are disjoint and their union has size
$R=F_p(m_q-F_q)+(m_p-F_p)F_q$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[The real wall is at $\max(p,q)$]
If $B\ge m_p$ and $B\ge m_q$ then $F_p=m_p$, $F_q=m_q$ and $R=0$: every trial is dead.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No wall at $\min(p,q)$]
Suppose $m_q\ge2$ and every prime factor of $m_q$ exceeds $B'$, with $0<B\le B'$ (the
mod-$q$ side is inert, $F_q=1$ at both bounds). Then $R$ at $B$ is at most $R$ at $B'$:
raising the bound never costs successes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inertness gives $R=F_p(m_q-1)+(m_p-F_p)$. With $x=\gcd(m_p,k(B))\le y=\gcd(m_p,k(B'))
\le m_p$ the claim reduces to $x(m_q-1)+(m_p-x)\le y(m_q-1)+(m_p-y)$, which holds since
$y-x\le (y-x)(m_q-1)$ for $m_q\ge2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Minimal witness]
With $m_p=m_q=2$: the reveal count is $2$ at $B=1$ and $0$ at $B=2$, the drop occurring
exactly when the bound covers both orders.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Channels redistribute]
With $m_p=4$, $m_q=6$, raising $B$ from $2$ to $3$ takes $|\mathrm{found}_p|$ from $8$
to $0$: those eight trials moved into the dead block when the mod-$q$ side began firing.
Monotonicity holds for the firing counts and for the reveal count under inertness, not
for individual channels.
\end{proposition}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{ledger} maps the firing pattern of a trial --- which of the two coordinates
fired --- to a recorded outcome; it is \emph{faithful} when injective. The
\emph{canonical} ledger records the four separated outcomes; the \emph{wall} ledger
records \emph{dead} whenever the $p$-side fires, regardless of the $q$-side.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Faithfulness dichotomy]
The canonical ledger is faithful; the wall ledger is not, collapsing
$(\text{fire},\text{fire})$ with $(\text{fire},\text{inert})$. On the pattern
$(\text{fire},\text{inert})$ --- exactly the pattern produced with $B$ past the Hasse
window on the $p$-side and the $q$-side inert --- the canonical ledger records
found$_p$ while the wall ledger records dead.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A finite check over the four patterns.
\end{proof}

Hence a reported wall at the smaller prime is, verbatim, the image of one non-injective
conflation, contradicted by the counts of Theorem~\ref{thm:blocks}.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Shadow-instrumented rho}
Run the method modulo $N$ while watching the mod-$p$ shadow: store each shadow value
with its index, and on a repeat return the index together with
$\gcd(x_n-x_i \bmod N,\,N)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow} the recorded shadow sequence is
independent of the cofactor, and when the shadow closes strictly before the mod-$N$ run
does, the two colliding states are congruent modulo $p$ but distinct modulo $N$, so the
gcd is a nontrivial proper divisor of $N$ divisible by $p$. The cost is $O(T)$ steps
with $T\le p$ and heuristically $T=\Theta(\sqrt p)$.

\subsection{Exact ledger evaluation}
Given $m_p,m_q,B$, compute $k(B)$, the two firing counts by gcd, and then the four block
sizes and the reveal count in closed form: $O(B\log B)$ for the scalar plus $O(1)$ gcds.
A wall claim is exactly the assertion $R=0$.

\subsection{Locality diagnostic}
Fix $p$, sweep $q$ over several octaves, take medians over a fixed number of independent
draws per cell, and report the ratio of the largest to the smallest median. Single draws
are statistically inadequate: rho's per-cell cost legitimately spans an order of
magnitude.

\section{Discussion}

Practitioners choose a factoring method by the expected size of the factor rather than
by the size of $N$; Theorem~\ref{thm:nat} shows why this rule is a law. The
cryptographic contrapositive is that a modulus is safe only to the extent that its
smallest factor is large: a $2048$-bit modulus with a $60$-bit prime inside is a
$60$-bit problem to any factor-local method.

Both negative results here concern accounting rather than dynamics. Rigidity says a cost
ledger that refuses to read the factor buys triviality; faithfulness says a ledger that
conflates two firing patterns can manufacture a phenomenon the underlying counts
contradict. Treating the ledger as a first-class object --- a map from what a run can
observe to what it records, faithfulness meaning injectivity --- turns both questions
into short finite arguments.

Two limitations deserve emphasis. Cofactor flatness concerns the number of state
updates, not machine operations: arithmetic modulo a larger $N$ is intrinsically more
expensive. And factor boundedness by $p$ is sharp in the worst case
(Remark~\ref{rem:speed}); only the birthday heuristic, not a theorem, gives $\sqrt p$
for the quadratic map.

\section{Future directions}

\emph{Naturality obstruction for sub-exponential methods.} Every method proved
factor-local here has cost bounded by the size of the state space it is natural over.
This suggests a dichotomy: sub-exponential behaviour must come either from enlarging the
state space (elliptic curves supply a family of groups of order near $p$, one of which
may be smooth) or from abandoning naturality (sieve methods, whose cost is genuinely a
function of $N$). An obstruction theorem would explain the measured slope $1.13$ as a
finite-window artefact of exactly this trade.

\emph{Quantifying seed luck.} The intrinsic cost is a deterministic function of the pair
(prime, seed). An exact distributional statement over seeds would convert the
experimental flatness claim into a sharp confidence statement.

\emph{Robust rigidity.} A version of the rigidity theorem tolerating flatness only to
within a factor $\lambda$ would apply directly to measured data.

\emph{Faithfulness as an audit tool.} Any claim of the form ``the method dies at
parameter $X$'' can be tested by asking whether the recording map is injective on the
firing patterns produced near $X$. A general calculus of ledgers, with composition and
refinement, would make such audits mechanical.

\emph{Multi-prime ledgers.} For $r$ factors there are $2^r$ firing patterns; the reveal
count is the total minus the all-fire and no-fire blocks, and the wall moves to the
largest prime. Determining which conflations are harmless in that setting is the natural
next step.

\section{Conclusion}

Factor locality is an algebraic fact, not an empirical regularity. A method natural in
the ring has a mod-$p$ shadow equal to the mod-$p$ run, so the cofactor cannot enter and
the cost is exactly flat and bounded by $p$. Conversely a method whose ledger reads only
the modulus can be flat only if constant, so trial division's behaviour is forced. The
elliptic curve method is local by an exact count: its stage-1 rate is $\gcd(m,k(B))/m$,
its curve count is bounded by the Hasse ceiling of the factor, antitone in the bound and
equal to one past the window --- so the only genuine degeneracy wall lies at the larger
prime, and any wall reported at the smaller one is an artefact of a non-injective
ledger.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import exp, gcd, isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Collision time: the cost model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def collision_time(step: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, modulus: int) -> int:
    """First index n such that state n equals a strictly earlier state.

    The state space has `modulus` elements, so by pigeonhole the answer is at most
    `modulus`.
    """
    seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    x = x0 % modulus
    n = 0
    while x not in seen:
        seen[x] = n
        x = step(x) % modulus
        n += 1
    return n


def rho_step(c: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """One Pollard-rho update x -> x^2 + c, valid in any commutative ring."""
    return lambda x: x * x + c


def shadow_orbit(f: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, N: int, p: int, length: int) -> List[int]:
    """The mod-p shadow of the orbit computed modulo N."""
    out: List[int] = []
    x = x0 % N
    for _ in range(length):
        out.append(x % p)
        x = f(x) % N
    return out


def intrinsic_orbit(f: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, p: int, length: int) -> List[int]:
    """The orbit computed entirely modulo p."""
    out: List[int] = []
    x = x0 % p
    for _ in range(length):
        out.append(x)
        x = f(x) % p
    return out


def shadow_collision_time(f: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, N: int, p: int) -> int:
    """Cost of a run modulo N while hunting p: collision time of the mod-p shadow."""
    seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    x = x0 % N
    n = 0
    while (x % p) not in seen:
        seen[x % p] = n
        x = f(x) % N
        n += 1
    return n


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Trial division
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def min_fac(n: int) -> int:
    """Least prime factor of n >= 2."""
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return d
        d += 2
    return n


def trial_steps(n: int) -> int:
    """Cost of ascending trial division: one failed test per candidate below minFac."""
    return min_fac(n) - 1


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Elliptic curve stage-1 ledger
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def stage1_scalar(B: int) -> int:
    """k(B) = lcm(1, 2, ..., B)."""
    k = 1
    for i in range(1, B + 1):
        k = k * i // gcd(k, i)
    return k


def firing_count(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Number of residues a < m with m | k*a.  Equals gcd(m, k)."""
    return gcd(m, k)


def firing_count_bruteforce(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for a in range(m) if (k * a) % m == 0)


def hasse_ceil(p: int) -> int:
    """Integer ceiling of the Hasse window: p + 3 + 2*floor(sqrt(p))."""
    return p + 3 + 2 * isqrt(p)


def expected_curves(m: int, B: int) -> int:
    """Expected number of curves: reciprocal of the stage-1 firing rate."""
    return m // gcd(m, stage1_scalar(B))


def blocks(m_p: int, m_q: int, k: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    """(dead, found_p, found_q, nothing) counts of a two-prime stage-1 run."""
    fp, fq = gcd(m_p, k), gcd(m_q, k)
    return (fp * fq, fp * (m_q - fq), (m_p - fp) * fq, (m_p - fp) * (m_q - fq))


def reveal_count(m_p: int, m_q: int, k: int) -> int:
    dead, found_p, found_q, nothing = blocks(m_p, m_q, k)
    del dead, nothing
    return found_p + found_q


def blocks_bruteforce(m_p: int, m_q: int, k: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    dead = found_p = found_q = nothing = 0
    for a in range(m_p):
        for b in range(m_q):
            fp = (k * a) % m_p == 0
            fq = (k * b) % m_q == 0
            if fp and fq:
                dead += 1
            elif fp:
                found_p += 1
            elif fq:
                found_q += 1
            else:
                nothing += 1
    return dead, found_p, found_q, nothing


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Birthday bound
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def birthday_product(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Probability that k uniform draws from Z/p are pairwise distinct."""
    prob = 1.0
    for i in range(k):
        prob *= 1.0 - i / p
    return prob


def birthday_bound(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """exp(-k(k-1)/(2p)), an upper bound for the product above."""
    return exp(-k * (k - 1) / (2.0 * p))

def next_prime(n: int) -> int:
    def is_prime(x: int) -> bool:
        if x < 2:
            return False
        if x % 2 == 0:
            return x == 2

        while d * d <= x:
            if x % d == 0:
                return False
            d += 2
        return True

    while not is_prime(n):
        n += 1
    return n

from __future__ import annotations

from math import exp, gcd, isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Collision time: the cost model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def collision_time(step: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, modulus: int) -> int:
    """First index n such that state n equals a strictly earlier state.

    The state space has `modulus` elements, so by pigeonhole the answer is at most
    `modulus`.
    """
    seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    x = x0 % modulus
    n = 0
    while x not in seen:
        seen[x] = n
        x = step(x) % modulus
        n += 1
    return n


def rho_step(c: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """One Pollard-rho update x -> x^2 + c, valid in any commutative ring."""
    return lambda x: x * x + c


def shadow_orbit(f: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, N: int, p: int, length: int) -> List[int]:
    """The mod-p shadow of the orbit computed modulo N."""
    out: List[int] = []
    x = x0 % N
    for _ in range(length):
        out.append(x % p)
        x = f(x) % N
    return out


def intrinsic_orbit(f: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, p: int, length: int) -> List[int]:
    """The orbit computed entirely modulo p."""
    out: List[int] = []
    x = x0 % p
    for _ in range(length):
        out.append(x)
        x = f(x) % p
    return out


def shadow_collision_time(f: Callable[[int], int], x0: int, N: int, p: int) -> int:
    """Cost of a run modulo N while hunting p: collision time of the mod-p shadow."""
    seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    x = x0 % N
    n = 0
    while (x % p) not in seen:
        seen[x % p] = n
        x = f(x) % N
        n += 1
    return n


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Trial division
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def min_fac(n: int) -> int:
    """Least prime factor of n >= 2."""
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return d
        d += 2
    return n


def trial_steps(n: int) -> int:
    """Cost of ascending trial division: one failed test per candidate below minFac."""
    return min_fac(n) - 1


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Elliptic curve stage-1 ledger
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def stage1_scalar(B: int) -> int:
    """k(B) = lcm(1, 2, ..., B)."""
    k = 1
    for i in range(1, B + 1):
        k = k * i // gcd(k, i)
    return k


def firing_count(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Number of residues a < m with m | k*a.  Equals gcd(m, k)."""
    return gcd(m, k)


def firing_count_bruteforce(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for a in range(m) if (k * a) % m == 0)


def hasse_ceil(p: int) -> int:
    """Integer ceiling of the Hasse window: p + 3 + 2*floor(sqrt(p))."""
    return p + 3 + 2 * isqrt(p)


def expected_curves(m: int, B: int) -> int:
    """Expected number of curves: reciprocal of the stage-1 firing rate."""
    return m // gcd(m, stage1_scalar(B))


def blocks(m_p: int, m_q: int, k: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    """(dead, found_p, found_q, nothing) counts of a two-prime stage-1 run."""
    fp, fq = gcd(m_p, k), gcd(m_q, k)
    return (fp * fq, fp * (m_q - fq), (m_p - fp) * fq, (m_p - fp) * (m_q - fq))


def reveal_count(m_p: int, m_q: int, k: int) -> int:
    dead, found_p, found_q, nothing = blocks(m_p, m_q, k)
    del dead, nothing
    return found_p + found_q


def blocks_bruteforce(m_p: int, m_q: int, k: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    dead = found_p = found_q = nothing = 0
    for a in range(m_p):
        for b in range(m_q):
            fp = (k * a) % m_p == 0
            fq = (k * b) % m_q == 0
            if fp and fq:
                dead += 1
            elif fp:
                found_p += 1
            elif fq:
                found_q += 1
            else:
                nothing += 1
    return dead, found_p, found_q, nothing


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Birthday bound
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def birthday_product(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Probability that k uniform draws from Z/p are pairwise distinct."""
    prob = 1.0
    for i in range(k):
        prob *= 1.0 - i / p
    return prob


def birthday_bound(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """exp(-k(k-1)/(2p)), an upper bound for the product above."""
    return exp(-k * (k - 1) / (2.0 * p))

        if x < 2:

        if x % 2 == 0:

            d += 2
        return True

class RhoReport(NamedTuple):

    modulus_cost: Optional[int]  # collision time of the mod-N run, if reached
    factor: Optional[int]     # nontrivial proper divisor of N, if revealed
    cofactor_independent: bool  # True: the shadow trace never consulted N/p


def shadow_rho(N: int, p: int, c: int = 1, x0: int = 2,
               max_steps: Optional[int] = None) -> RhoReport:
    """Run x -> x^2 + c modulo N, instrumented by its mod-p shadow.

    Preconditions: p is a prime divisor of N, 2 <= p < N.
    Cost: O(T) ring operations with T <= p; heuristically T = Theta(sqrt(p)).

        raise ValueError("p must divide N")
    cap = max_steps if max_steps is not None else p + 1
    step: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: (x * x + c) % N

    shadow_seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    states: Dict[int, int] = {}
    mod_n_seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    x = x0 % N
    n = 0
    shadow_cost: Optional[int] = None
    modulus_cost: Optional[int] = None
    factor: Optional[int] = None

    while n <= cap:
        s = x % p
        if shadow_cost is None and s in shadow_seen:
            shadow_cost = n
            earlier = states[shadow_seen[s]]
            if earlier != x:                     # shadow strictly faster than mod-N run
                d = gcd(abs(x - earlier), N)
                if 1 < d < N:
                    factor = d
            break
        if x in mod_n_seen and modulus_cost is None:
            modulus_cost = n
        shadow_seen.setdefault(s, n)
        mod_n_seen.setdefault(x, n)
        states[n] = x
        x = step(x)
        n += 1

    assert shadow_cost is not None, "pigeonhole guarantees a shadow collision by step p"
    return RhoReport(shadow_cost=shadow_cost, modulus_cost=modulus_cost,
                     factor=factor, cofactor_independent=True)

    """The same cost computed modulo p alone -- provably equal to shadow_cost."""
    seen = set()
    x, n = x0 % p, 0
    while x not in seen:
        seen.add(x)
        x = (x * x + c) % p
        n += 1
    return n

> **The one-sentence version.** If a composite $N = p\cdot q$ hides a small prime $p$,
> then Pollard's rho method and the elliptic curve method find it in a number of steps
> that depends on $p$ and *not at all* on $q$ — while trial division's cost is a
> function of $N$. This page explains why, exactly, and shows you where the boundary
> between the two behaviours lies.

---

## 1. A puzzle to start with

Take the prime $p = 4093$ and build composites $N = p\cdot q$ where $q$ runs over primes
near $2^{14}, 2^{15}, \dots, 2^{23}$. The largest of these numbers is eight million times
the smallest. Now run the same factoring method on each of them and count the *state
updates* — the number of times the algorithm applies its update rule.

Before you scroll: what do you expect the counts to look like?

{{interactive_demo:0}}

If you ran the sweep with the default settings, the rho column did not move. Not
"changed slowly" — it printed the same integer nine times. The trial-division column,
meanwhile, is pinned at $4092$ for these cofactors and would swing by three orders of
magnitude if you let $q$ be small. Something structural is going on.

---

## 2. Cost, defined once for every method

<details>
<summary><b>The definition we will use throughout (click to expand)</b></summary>

Every method here drives a state through a finite set. Pollard's rho iterates
$x \mapsto x^2 + c$ modulo $N$; the $p-1$ method iterates $x \mapsto x^k$; the elliptic
curve method multiplies a point by a scalar. In each case the run ends when the state
*repeats*.

**Definition.** A sequence $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ in a finite set *collides at time $n$*
if $s_n = s_i$ for some $i < n$. Its **collision time** $T(s)$ is the least such $n$.

Two facts fall out immediately:

- *Pigeonhole ceiling.* In a state space with $c$ elements, $T(s) \le c$ — the values
  $s_0, \dots, s_c$ cannot all be distinct.
- *Cost depends only on the trajectory.* If two runs produce the same sequence of
  states, they have the same cost, whatever machinery produced them.

That second fact is doing more work than it looks.
</details>

---

## 3. The shadow: the whole idea in one picture

Suppose $p \mid N$. Alongside the real run modulo $N$, watch the **shadow**: reduce
each state modulo $p$.

Reduction modulo $p$ is a *ring homomorphism* $\mathbb{Z}/N \to \mathbb{Z}/p$ — it
respects $+$ and $\times$. And the rho step $x \mapsto x^2 + c$ is built from nothing
but $+$ and $\times$. So *reduce-then-step* equals *step-then-reduce*, and by induction:

> **Shadow Theorem.** For any polynomial $f$ with integer coefficients, the mod-$p$
> reduction of the $n$-th state of the run modulo $N$ equals the $n$-th state of the
> run computed entirely modulo $p$.

The cofactor $q$ never entered the right-hand side, so it cannot influence it. Three
consequences follow at once, and they are the heart of everything below.

| consequence | statement | why |
|---|---|---|
| **cofactor flatness** | cost on $p q$ = cost on $p q'$, exactly | both equal the intrinsic mod-$p$ cost |
| **factor boundedness** | cost $\le p$ | pigeonhole in $\mathbb{Z}/p$ |
| **reveal** | a shadow collision that is not a full collision hands you a factor | the two states differ mod $N$ but agree mod $p$, so their difference shares the factor $p$ with $N$ |

{{algorithm:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Locality is not the same as speed</b></summary>

Locality says the cost is a function of $p$. It does *not* say the function is small.
The successor map $x \mapsto x+1$ modulo $p$ is just as natural in the ring, hence just
as cofactor flat — but its orbit visits every residue before repeating, so its cost is
exactly $p$: the pigeonhole bound, attained. Try selecting it in the explorer above.

The square-root behaviour of the rho map is a *statistical* bonus on top of locality,
governed by the birthday phenomenon: if $k$ successive states behaved like independent
uniform draws, the probability of no repeat would be
$$\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{i}{p}\right) \le \exp\!\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{2p}\right),$$
which crosses $1/2$ near $k \approx 1.18\sqrt p$. At $p = 4093$ that is $76$ steps; the
real orbit of $x^2+1$ from $x_0=2$ closes at step $70$.
</details>

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 4. The mechanism has a name: naturality

Polynomials are not the point; *naturality* is. Call a state update **uniform** if the
same formula defines it in every commutative ring and it commutes with every ring
homomorphism. Polynomial maps qualify. So does $x \mapsto x^k$, the exponentiation step
inside the $p-1$ method.

> **Locality-from-Naturality Theorem.** Every uniform method is cofactor flat and costs
> at most $p$.

So the flatness of rho and the $p-1$ method is not a lucky empirical fact about two
algorithms. It is a corollary of an algebraic property those algorithms have for
entirely unrelated design reasons. Read an interesting slogan out of it: **locality is
naturality**.

---

## 5. The other side of the boundary

{{visualization:0}}

Trial division tests $2, 3, 4, \dots$ until something divides, so its cost is
$\mathrm{minFac}(N) - 1$. On the stratum where the hunted prime *is* the least factor,
that is exactly $p-1$ — perfectly linear, matching the measured slope $1.09$ per
$\log_2 p$ against rho's $0.45$. But hold $p = 4093$ fixed and change only the cofactor:

$$\mathrm{cost}(4093\cdot 3) = 2, \qquad \mathrm{cost}(4093\cdot 4093) = 4092.$$

Is that an artefact of this particular algorithm? No — and this is the most surprising
theorem on the page.

<details>
<summary><b>The Rigidity Theorem, with its three-line proof</b></summary>

Call a cost model **modulus-determined** if its ledger never reads the hunted factor:
$\mathrm{cost}(N,p) = \mathrm{cost}(N,p')$ for all $p, p'$. Trial division is the
archetype — it cannot know in advance which factor it will hit.

> **Rigidity Theorem.** A modulus-determined, cofactor-flat cost model is *constant on
> composites*: it assigns the same value to every product $a\cdot b$ of positive
> integers.

*Proof.* Take composites $ab$ and $cd$.
1. By flatness with hunted factor $a$ and cofactors $b$ and $cd$:
   $\mathrm{cost}(ab) = \mathrm{cost}(a(cd))$.
2. $a(cd) = (cd)a$, and modulus-determinedness lets us re-label the hunted factor as
   $cd$.
3. By flatness with hunted factor $cd$ and cofactors $a$ and $1$:
   $\mathrm{cost}((cd)a) = \mathrm{cost}(cd\cdot 1) = \mathrm{cost}(cd)$. $\blacksquare$

So a method that reads only the modulus can be flat *only by being trivial*. Trial
division's non-flatness needs no counterexample; it is forced. Conversely, the rho
ledger is provably not modulus-determined — it costs $1$ step at $p=3$ and $70$ at
$p=4093$ — which is exactly the licence rigidity says a nontrivial flat model must have.
</details>

{{algorithm:2}}

---

## 6. Elliptic curves: locality by counting

The elliptic curve method reaches locality by a different road. Stage 1 forms the
scalar $k(B) = \operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,B)$ and multiplies a point by it. Modulo a
prime $p$ the point lives in the group of a curve over $\mathbb{F}_p$, of order $m$
within $2\sqrt p$ of $p$ by [Hasse's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves).

Modulo $N = pq$, the Chinese remainder theorem makes a random point a uniform pair of
residues, one per prime, with group orders $m$ and $m'$. Count the joint states whose
$p$-coordinate is annihilated: there are $\gcd(m, k)\cdot m'$ of them, so the success
rate is
$$\frac{\gcd(m,k)\,m'}{m\,m'} \;=\; \frac{\gcd(m,k)}{m}.$$

The cofactor order $m'$ **cancels identically**. The expected curve count
$m/\gcd(m,k(B))$ is bounded by the Hasse ceiling $p + 3 + 2\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$ — a
function of $p$ alone — never increases as $B$ grows, and equals exactly $1$ once $B$
passes the top of the Hasse window.

That last clause matters, because it contradicts a claim you may have met: that pushing
$B$ too far produces a wall at which every curve degenerates. Let us settle it by
looking at the actual counts.

---

## 7. The ledger room: where the wall really is

{{interactive_demo:1}}

Play with it before reading on. Set the two group orders, slide the bound, and switch
the ledger from *faithful* to *conflating*.

<details>
<summary><b>The exact block counts behind the colours</b></summary>

Write $F_p = \gcd(m_p,k)$ and $F_q = \gcd(m_q,k)$ for the firing counts. The four
outcomes have sizes that are pure products:

$$|\text{dead}| = F_pF_q,\quad |\text{found }p| = F_p(m_q-F_q),$$
$$|\text{found }q| = (m_p-F_p)F_q,\quad |\text{nothing}| = (m_p-F_p)(m_q-F_q),$$

and they sum to $m_pm_q$ — every trial is accounted for. The **reveal count** is
$$R = F_p(m_q-F_q) + (m_p-F_p)F_q.$$

Because $F_p, F_q \ge 1$, we get $R = 0$ **exactly** when $F_p = m_p$ and $F_q = m_q$:
the scalar must annihilate *both* groups. A bound $B \ge \max(m_p,m_q)$ always achieves
that, and no bound below $\min(m_p,m_q)$ ever can. Hence: the real wall sits at the
*larger* prime. Furthermore, while the $q$-side stays inert ($F_q = 1$), the reveal
count is monotone increasing in $B$ — raising the bound never costs successes.

The smallest witness of the real wall is charming: two groups of order $2$. At $B=1$
both trials reveal a factor; at $B=2$ neither does.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>How a non-injective ledger manufactures a wall</b></summary>

Think of a **ledger** as a map from the *firing pattern* of a trial — which of the two
coordinates degenerated — to a recorded outcome. Call it **faithful** when it is
injective.

- The four-way separated ledger is faithful: four patterns, four distinct records.
- The ledger that files *any* $p$-side firing as a death is not: it collapses
  (fire, fire) with (fire, inert).

And (fire, inert) is precisely the pattern produced in the regime where a wall was
reported — bound past the $p$-side window, $q$-side still inert. There the faithful
ledger records "factor $p$ found"; the conflating one records "dead". The wall sentence
is the image of that single misfiling, nothing more.

There is a real subtlety the separation exposes: the found-$p$ channel *alone* is not
monotone. With orders $4$ and $6$, raising $B$ from $2$ to $3$ takes the found-$p$ count
from $8$ to $0$ — because those eight trials moved into the dead block when the $q$-side
began firing. Channels redistribute; only a faithful ledger lets you see it.
</details>

{{algorithm:1}}

## 9. What to take away

1. **Choose a method by the size of the factor you hope for, not by the size of $N$.**
   That rule of thumb is a theorem: naturality in the ring *is* cofactor flatness.
2. **A modulus is only as safe as its smallest factor.** A $2048$-bit modulus hiding a
   $60$-bit prime is a $60$-bit problem to a factor-local method. This is why key
   generation insists on balanced primes.
3. **Cost models are mathematical objects with their own theorems.** A ledger that
   refuses to read the factor buys triviality (rigidity); a ledger that conflates two
   observable outcomes can manufacture a phenomenon the underlying counts contradict
   (faithfulness). Auditing the accounting is part of doing the mathematics.

### Where to read further

- [Pollard's rho algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollard%27s_rho_algorithm) — the

- [Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves) —
  the window that bounds the curve count by a function of $p$.
- [The birthday problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem) — where the

/-!
# Method locality: which factoring methods track the factor, and which track the modulus

Round-28 experiment "METHOD-LOCALITY" (fixed prime `p = 4093`, cofactor `q` grown
`2^14 → 2^23`, 9 draws per cell) reported the verdict
**THE-METHODS-ARE-FACTOR-LOCAL**: the observed step counts of Pollard ρ and of ECM
stayed flat (`×1.40` and `×2.16` median spread) while the modulus grew by `2^23`,
whereas the `p`-scaling slopes separated (`ρ ≈ 0.45`, trial division `≈ 1.09` per
`log₂ p`).

This file turns that verdict into theorems, and in doing so *sharpens* it, because
the informal phrase "factor-local" conflates two genuinely different properties:

* **cofactor flatness** — the cost of a run on `N = p·q` does not depend on `q` at
  all; and
* **factor boundedness** — the cost is bounded by a function of `p` alone.

The main results are:

* `rhoSeq_reduce`, `rho_modp_time_eq`, `rho_cofactor_flat` — Pollard ρ is *exactly*
  cofactor flat.  The ρ iteration is a polynomial map, hence commutes with the ring
  map `ZMod N →+* ZMod p`; the mod-`p` collision time of the run performed modulo
  `N` therefore equals the collision time of the run performed modulo `p` itself and
  is literally independent of the cofactor.  The measured `×1.40` spread is method
  luck (different seeds), not cofactor dependence: the theorem gives ratio `1`.
* `rhoTime_le_factor` — that cost is at most `p`: a factor-bounded method.
* `rho_collision_reveals_factor` — a mod-`p` collision that is not a mod-`N`
  collision yields a *proper* divisor of `N` that is a multiple of `p`.
* `trialSteps_eq_of_le`, `trialSteps_le_of_prime_dvd` — ascending trial division is
  factor bounded (`≤ p - 1` for every prime factor `p`), and on the stratum where
  `p` is the least factor its cost is *exactly* `p - 1`: the "definition face",
  slope `1` per `p`, matching the measured `1.09`.
* `trial_not_cofactor_flat` — but trial division is **not** cofactor flat: with the
  factor `p = 4093` held fixed, cost `2` at `q = 3` versus cost `4092` at
  `q = 4093`.  This is the precise sense in which the verdict is right, and
  `trial_locality_dichotomy` states the resulting dichotomy.
* `rho_time_4093`, `rho_beats_trial_at_4093` — the experimental anchor, verified by
  kernel computation: the ρ orbit of `x ↦ x² + 1` from `x₀ = 2` modulo `4093` first
  repeats at step `70` (`√4093 ≈ 64`), i.e. `58×` cheaper than the `4092` trial
  divisions, and `70 ≤ 2√4093`.
* `collTime_succ_eq_self` — a *critique* of the `0.45` slope: the birthday exponent
  is not a worst-case theorem.  For the successor map on `ZMod p` the collision time
  is exactly `p`, so `√p` is a statement about typical maps, not all of them.
* `birthday_prod_le_exp`, `birthday_half_4093` — the honest form of the `√p` law: in
  the uniform model the no-collision probability after `k` draws is at most
  `exp(-k(k-1)/2p)`, which at `p = 4093` is below `1/2` already at `k = 76` — the
  measured `70` sits exactly in this window.
-/

namespace MethodLocality

open Finset

/-! ## 1. A collision-time calculus

Every method in the round-28 plane is a search for a repetition in a sequence of
states.  We measure cost as the first index at which the sequence repeats a value
it has already taken.
-/

variable {β : Type*}

/-- The sequence `s` collides at time `n` if some strictly earlier term equals `s n`. -/
def SeqColl (s : ℕ → β) (n : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ i < n, s i = s n

/-- A sequence into a finite type must collide. -/
theorem exists_seqColl [Finite β] (s : ℕ → β) : ∃ n, SeqColl s n := by
  obtain ⟨i, j, hij, h⟩ := Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite s
  rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hij with h1 | h1
  · exact ⟨j, i, h1, h⟩
  · exact ⟨i, j, h1, h.symm⟩

/-- **Cost of a search**: the first time the state sequence repeats. -/
noncomputable def collTime (s : ℕ → β) : ℕ := sInf {n | SeqColl s n}

theorem collTime_le {s : ℕ → β} {n : ℕ} (h : SeqColl s n) : collTime s ≤ n := Nat.sInf_le h

theorem collTime_mem [Finite β] (s : ℕ → β) : SeqColl s (collTime s) := by
  have : collTime s ∈ {n | SeqColl s n} := Nat.sInf_mem (exists_seqColl s)
  simpa [Set.mem_setOf_eq] using this

theorem not_seqColl_of_lt_collTime {s : ℕ → β} {n : ℕ} (h : n < collTime s) :
    ¬ SeqColl s n := fun hn => absurd (collTime_le hn) (not_le.mpr h)

/-- Cost is determined by the state sequence alone. -/
theorem collTime_congr {s t : ℕ → β} (h : ∀ n, s n = t n) : collTime s = collTime t := by
  simp [funext h]

theorem collTime_eq {s : ℕ → β} {n : ℕ} [Finite β] (h : SeqColl s n)
    (hmin : ∀ m < n, ¬ SeqColl s m) : collTime s = n :=
  le_antisymm (collTime_le h) (Nat.le_of_not_lt fun hlt => hmin _ hlt (collTime_mem s))

/-- The pigeonhole ceiling: a search in a state space of size `c` costs at most `c`. -/
theorem collTime_le_card [Fintype β] (s : ℕ → β) : collTime s ≤ Fintype.card β := by
  classical
  obtain ⟨i, hi, j, hj, hij, h⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt_of_maps_to (s := Finset.range (Fintype.card β + 1))
      (t := (Finset.univ : Finset β)) (by simp) (f := s) (fun n _ => Finset.mem_univ _)
  simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hi hj
  rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hij with h1 | h1
  · exact le_trans (collTime_le ⟨i, h1, h⟩) (by omega)
  · exact le_trans (collTime_le ⟨j, h1, h.symm⟩) (by omega)

/-! ## 2. Pollard ρ is a polynomial map, hence equivariant under reduction -/

/-- One Pollard-ρ step `x ↦ x² + c`, in an arbitrary commutative ring. -/
def rhoStep {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (c x : R) : R := x * x + c

/-- The ρ orbit of the seed `x₀`. -/
def rhoSeq {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (c x0 : R) (n : ℕ) : R := (rhoStep c)^[n] x0

theorem map_rhoStep {R S : Type*} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] (φ : R →+* S) (c x : R) :
    φ (rhoStep c x) = rhoStep (φ c) (φ x) := by
  simp [rhoStep]

/-- **Equivariance.**  A ring map intertwines the ρ orbits. -/
theorem map_rhoSeq {R S : Type*} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] (φ : R →+* S) (c x0 : R) (n : ℕ) :
    φ (rhoSeq c x0 n) = rhoSeq (φ c) (φ x0) n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp [rhoSeq]
  | succ n ih =>
      simp only [rhoSeq, Function.iterate_succ_apply'] at *
      rw [map_rhoStep, ih]

/-- **The mod-`p` shadow of a mod-`N` run is the mod-`p` run.**  The cofactor never
enters: the reduction of the orbit computed modulo `N` is the orbit computed
modulo `p` from the reduced seed. -/
theorem rhoSeq_reduce {p N : ℕ} [NeZero p] (h : p ∣ N) (c x0 : ℤ) (n : ℕ) :
    (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n)
      = rhoSeq ((c : ZMod p)) ((x0 : ZMod p)) n := by
  rw [map_rhoSeq]
  simp [map_intCast]

/-- The cost of Pollard ρ run modulo `N` when hunting the factor `p`: the first time
the mod-`p` shadow of the orbit repeats. -/
noncomputable def rhoTime (p N : ℕ) [NeZero p] (h : p ∣ N) (c x0 : ℤ) : ℕ :=
  collTime (fun n => (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n))

/-- The intrinsic, modulus-free ρ cost attached to the factor `p` alone. -/
noncomputable def rhoTimeAtFactor (p : ℕ) (c x0 : ℤ) : ℕ :=
  collTime (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod p)) ((x0 : ZMod p)))

/-- **Factor locality of ρ (H1).**  The cost of the mod-`N` run equals the cost of the
mod-`p` run: the modulus has been eliminated from the ledger. -/
theorem rho_time_eq_factor_time {p N : ℕ} [NeZero p] (h : p ∣ N) (c x0 : ℤ) :
    rhoTime p N h c x0 = rhoTimeAtFactor p c x0 :=
  collTime_congr (rhoSeq_reduce h c x0)

/-- **Cofactor flatness, exactly.**  Two runs with the same factor `p` and the same
integer seed, on two arbitrary cofactors, cost the same — flatness ratio `1`, against
the measured median ratio `1.40` over `2^23` of cofactor growth. -/
theorem rho_cofactor_flat {p q q' : ℕ} [NeZero p] (c x0 : ℤ)
    (h : p ∣ p * q) (h' : p ∣ p * q') :
    rhoTime p (p * q) h c x0 = rhoTime p (p * q') h' c x0 := by
  rw [rho_time_eq_factor_time, rho_time_eq_factor_time]

/-- **Factor boundedness of ρ.**  The cost never exceeds `p`, whatever the modulus. -/
theorem rhoTime_le_factor {p N : ℕ} [NeZero p] (h : p ∣ N) (c x0 : ℤ) :
    rhoTime p N h c x0 ≤ p := by
  rw [rho_time_eq_factor_time, rhoTimeAtFactor]
  simpa using collTime_le_card (β := ZMod p) (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod p)) ((x0 : ZMod p)))

/-! ## 3. A mod-`p` collision is a factor -/

/-- **Reveal.**  A pair of states that agree modulo `p` but differ modulo `N` hands
over a proper divisor of `N` divisible by `p`; since `p` is prime the gcd is a
nontrivial factor. -/
theorem factor_revealed {p N a b : ℕ} (hp : 2 ≤ p) (hpN : p ∣ N) (hba : b < a) (haN : a < N)
    (hcong : a ≡ b [MOD p]) :
    p ∣ Nat.gcd (a - b) N ∧ Nat.gcd (a - b) N ∣ N ∧ Nat.gcd (a - b) N < N ∧
      2 ≤ Nat.gcd (a - b) N := by
  have hdvd : p ∣ a - b := (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' hba.le).mp hcong.symm
  have hg : Nat.gcd (a - b) N ∣ N := Nat.gcd_dvd_right _ _
  have hpos : 0 < a - b := by omega
  have hlt : a - b < N := by omega
  have hpg : p ∣ Nat.gcd (a - b) N := Nat.dvd_gcd hdvd hpN
  have hgpos : 0 < Nat.gcd (a - b) N := Nat.gcd_pos_of_pos_left _ hpos
  refine ⟨hpg, hg, lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.le_of_dvd hpos (Nat.gcd_dvd_left _ _)) hlt, ?_⟩
  exact le_trans hp (Nat.le_of_dvd hgpos hpg)

/-- The ρ states themselves: a mod-`p` collision of the mod-`N` orbit is a congruence
between the two integer representatives. -/
theorem rho_collision_reveals_factor {p N : ℕ} [NeZero p] [NeZero N] (hp : 2 ≤ p) (h : p ∣ N)
    (c x0 : ℤ) {i n : ℕ}
    (hcoll : (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) i)
      = (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n))
    (hne : (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n).val
      < (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) i).val) :
    p ∣ Nat.gcd ((rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) i).val
        - (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n).val) N := by
  set a := (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) i) with ha
  set b := (rhoSeq ((c : ZMod N)) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n) with hb
  have hcast : ∀ z : ZMod N, (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) z = ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod p) := by
    intro z
    have hz : ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod N) = z := ZMod.natCast_rightInverse z
    calc (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) z
        = (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod N) := by rw [hz]
      _ = ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod p) := map_natCast _ _
  have hcong : a.val ≡ b.val [MOD p] := by
    have := hcoll
    rw [hcast a, hcast b] at this
    exact (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff _ _ _).mp this
  have haN : a.val < N := ZMod.val_lt a
  exact (factor_revealed hp h hne haN hcong).1

/-! ## 4. The birthday exponent is not a worst case

Critique of the measured slope `0.45`: a state-space search *can* cost the full `p`.
-/

theorem succ_iterate {p : ℕ} (x0 : ZMod p) (n : ℕ) :
    (fun x : ZMod p => x + 1)^[n] x0 = x0 + (n : ZMod p) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih => rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply', ih]; push_cast; ring

/-- **Worst-case locality without the birthday gain.**  The orbit of the successor
map on `ZMod p` visits every residue before repeating: the cost is exactly `p`, not
`√p`.  So the `0.45` exponent is a statement about typical quadratic maps, never a
theorem about all state maps of the same state space. -/
theorem collTime_succ_eq_self {p : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) (x0 : ZMod p) :
    collTime (fun n : ℕ => (fun x : ZMod p => x + 1)^[n] x0) = p := by
  haveI : NeZero p := ⟨hp.ne'⟩
  refine collTime_eq ⟨0, hp, ?_⟩ ?_
  · simp [succ_iterate]
  · rintro m hm ⟨i, him, hEq⟩
    simp only [succ_iterate] at hEq
    have h2 : ((i : ℕ) : ZMod p) = ((m : ℕ) : ZMod p) := add_left_cancel hEq
    have := (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff' i m p).mp h2
    rw [Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (by omega), Nat.mod_eq_of_lt (by omega)] at this
    omega

/-! ## 5. The birthday law in its honest (probabilistic) form -/

theorem sum_range_real (k : ℕ) : (∑ i ∈ Finset.range k, (i : ℝ)) = (k * (k - 1)) / 2 := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih => rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih]; push_cast; ring

/-- **Birthday bound.**  In the uniform model the probability that `k ≤ p` successive
states are pairwise distinct is `∏_{i<k}(1 - i/p) ≤ exp(-k(k-1)/2p)`; the search
therefore succeeds by `k ≍ √p` steps, which is the content of the `0.45` slope. -/
theorem birthday_prod_le_exp {p k : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) (hk : k ≤ p) :
    (∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (1 - (i : ℝ) / p)) ≤ Real.exp (-((k : ℝ) * (k - 1)) / (2 * p)) := by
  have hpR : (0 : ℝ) < p := by exact_mod_cast hp
  have hstep : ∀ i ∈ Finset.range k, (1 - (i : ℝ) / p) ≤ Real.exp (-((i : ℝ) / p)) := by
    intro i _
    have := Real.add_one_le_exp (-((i : ℝ) / p))
    linarith
  have hnonneg : ∀ i ∈ Finset.range k, (0 : ℝ) ≤ 1 - (i : ℝ) / p := by
    intro i hi
    simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hi
    have : (i : ℝ) ≤ p := by exact_mod_cast (le_of_lt (lt_of_lt_of_le hi hk))
    rw [sub_nonneg, div_le_one hpR]
    exact this
  calc (∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (1 - (i : ℝ) / p))
      ≤ ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, Real.exp (-((i : ℝ) / p)) := Finset.prod_le_prod hnonneg hstep
    _ = Real.exp (∑ i ∈ Finset.range k, (-((i : ℝ) / p))) := by rw [Real.exp_sum]
    _ = Real.exp (-((k : ℝ) * (k - 1)) / (2 * p)) := by
        congr 1
        rw [Finset.sum_neg_distrib, ← Finset.sum_div, sum_range_real]
        field_simp

/-- **The experimental window at the anchor prime.**  At `p = 4093` the uniform-model
survival probability is already below `1/2` at `k = 76`; the measured ρ time was
`70`. -/
theorem birthday_half_4093 : (∏ i ∈ Finset.range 76, (1 - (i : ℝ) / 4093)) ≤ 1 / 2 := by
  refine (birthday_prod_le_exp (p := 4093) (k := 76) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)).trans ?_
  have hlog : Real.log 2 < 0.6931471808 := Real.log_two_lt_d9
  have h2 : ((1 : ℝ) / 2) = Real.exp (-Real.log 2) := by
    rw [Real.exp_neg, Real.exp_log (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) < 2)]
    norm_num
  rw [h2]
  apply Real.exp_le_exp.mpr
  norm_num
  linarith

/-! ## 6. Trial division: the definition face -/

/-- Number of trial divisors `2, 3, …, minFac N` inspected by ascending trial
division before `N` gives up its least factor. -/
def trialSteps (N : ℕ) : ℕ := N.minFac - 1

/-- The inspected candidates below the least factor all fail — the cost really is the
count of tested divisors. -/
theorem trial_tests_fail {N d : ℕ} (hd : 2 ≤ d) (hlt : d < N.minFac) : ¬ d ∣ N := by
  intro hdvd
  have := Nat.minFac_le_of_dvd hd hdvd
  omega

theorem trialSteps_eq_card (N : ℕ) : trialSteps N = (Finset.Icc 2 N.minFac).card := by
  rcases Nat.lt_or_ge N.minFac 2 with h | h
  · interval_cases hm : N.minFac <;> simp [trialSteps, hm]
  · rw [Nat.card_Icc]
    simp [trialSteps]

theorem minFac_semiprime {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≤ q) :
    (p * q).minFac = p := by
  have hple := hp.two_le
  have hqle := hq.two_le
  have hle : (p * q).minFac ≤ p := Nat.minFac_le_of_dvd hple ⟨q, rfl⟩
  have hdvd : (p * q).minFac ∣ p * q := Nat.minFac_dvd _
  have hne : p * q ≠ 1 := by nlinarith
  have hprime : (p * q).minFac.Prime := Nat.minFac_prime hne
  rcases (Nat.Prime.dvd_mul hprime).mp hdvd with h | h
  · exact (Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hprime hp).mp h
  · have := (Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hprime hq).mp h
    omega

/-- **The definition face.**  On the stratum where the hunted prime is the least
factor, trial division costs exactly `p - 1`: slope `1` per `p`, the measured
`1.09`. -/
theorem trialSteps_eq_of_le {p q : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≤ q) :
    trialSteps (p * q) = p - 1 := by
  rw [trialSteps, minFac_semiprime hp hq hpq]

/-- **Factor boundedness of trial division.**  For *any* prime factor `p` of `N`, the
cost is at most `p - 1`. -/
theorem trialSteps_le_of_prime_dvd {N p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpN : p ∣ N) :
    trialSteps N ≤ p - 1 := by
  have := Nat.minFac_le_of_dvd hp.two_le hpN
  simp [trialSteps]
  omega

/-- **Exact linear law.**  Cost ratios across two least-factor strata are exactly the
ratios of the factors: no sub-linear gain is available to trial division. -/
theorem trial_linear_law {p q p' q' : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≤ q)
    (hp' : p'.Prime) (hq' : q'.Prime) (hpq' : p' ≤ q') :
    (p' - 1) * trialSteps (p * q) = (p - 1) * trialSteps (p' * q') := by
  rw [trialSteps_eq_of_le hp hq hpq, trialSteps_eq_of_le hp' hq' hpq', Nat.mul_comm]

/-- **Trial division is not cofactor flat.**  Holding the hunted factor at
`p = 4093`, the cost of trial division on `p·q` is `2` for `q = 3` and `4092` for
`q = 4093`: the cofactor, not the factor, decides.  Contrast `rho_cofactor_flat`. -/
theorem trial_not_cofactor_flat :
    trialSteps (4093 * 3) = 2 ∧ trialSteps (4093 * 4093) = 4092 ∧
      trialSteps (4093 * 3) ≠ trialSteps (4093 * 4093) := by
  have h3 : Nat.Prime 3 := by norm_num
  have h4093 : Nat.Prime 4093 := by norm_num
  have e1 : trialSteps (4093 * 3) = 2 := by
    rw [Nat.mul_comm]
    exact trialSteps_eq_of_le h3 h4093 (by norm_num)
  have e2 : trialSteps (4093 * 4093) = 4092 :=
    trialSteps_eq_of_le h4093 h4093 le_rfl
  exact ⟨e1, e2, by omega⟩

  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k, b ^ h + 1 = p * k := h_div
  have hk_bounds : 1 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ b ^ h - 1 := by

/-! ## 1. Uniform steps: naturality as a definition -/

/-- A **uniform step** is a state update defined simultaneously for all commutative
rings and commuting with every ring map: the algebraic form of "the method does not
look at the modulus". -/
structure UniformStep where
  /-- the state update on each commutative ring -/
  step : ∀ (R : Type) [CommRing R], R → R
  /-- naturality: ring maps intertwine the updates -/
  natural : ∀ {R S : Type} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] (φ : R →+* S) (x : R),
    φ (step R x) = step S (φ x)

/-- The orbit of a uniform step. -/
def UniformStep.orbit (M : UniformStep) (R : Type) [CommRing R] (x0 : R) (n : ℕ) : R :=
  (M.step R)^[n] x0

theorem UniformStep.map_orbit (M : UniformStep) {R S : Type} [CommRing R] [CommRing S]
    (φ : R →+* S) (x0 : R) (n : ℕ) : φ (M.orbit R x0 n) = M.orbit S (φ x0) n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp [UniformStep.orbit]
  | succ n ih =>
      simp only [UniformStep.orbit, Function.iterate_succ_apply'] at *
      rw [M.natural, ih]

/-- The mod-`p` shadow of a uniform run modulo `N` is the uniform run modulo `p`. -/
theorem UniformStep.orbit_reduce (M : UniformStep) {p N : ℕ} (h : p ∣ N) (x0 : ℤ) (n : ℕ) :

      = M.orbit (ZMod p) ((x0 : ZMod p)) n := by
  rw [M.map_orbit]
  simp [map_intCast]

/-- Cost of a uniform method run modulo `N` while hunting the factor `p`. -/
noncomputable def uniformTime (M : UniformStep) (p N : ℕ) (h : p ∣ N) (x0 : ℤ) : ℕ :=
  collTime (fun n => (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (M.orbit (ZMod N) ((x0 : ZMod N)) n))

/-- The intrinsic cost attached to the factor. -/
noncomputable def uniformTimeAtFactor (M : UniformStep) (p : ℕ) (x0 : ℤ) : ℕ :=
  collTime (M.orbit (ZMod p) ((x0 : ZMod p)))

theorem uniformTime_eq_factor_time (M : UniformStep) {p N : ℕ} (h : p ∣ N) (x0 : ℤ) :

theorem finset_gcd_fib (s : Finset ℕ) :

/-!
# Sorting: decision-tree entropy, reversible history, and Landauer work

Sorting distinct inputs has `n!` possible orderings.  This chapter separates three
quantities that are often conflated:

* the height of a binary comparison tree;
* the information erased by a many-to-one sorting map;
* the history space required to make that map reversible.

The same factorial controls all three, but raw comparison count does not itself measure
thermodynamic work: redundant comparisons may be inserted without changing the computed
map or its erased information.
-/

open Function

namespace SortingEntropyWork

/-- The shape of a binary comparison tree. -/
inductive ComparisonTree where
  | leaf : ComparisonTree
  | branch : ComparisonTree → ComparisonTree → ComparisonTree

namespace ComparisonTree

/-- Number of terminal transcripts. -/
def leaves : ComparisonTree → ℕ
  | leaf => 1
  | branch l r => leaves l + leaves r

/-- Worst-case number of comparisons. -/
def height : ComparisonTree → ℕ
  | leaf => 0
  | branch l r => 1 + max (height l) (height r)

/-- Insert `r` redundant comparison levels above a tree. -/
def pad : ℕ → ComparisonTree → ComparisonTree
  | 0, t => t
  | r + 1, t => branch (pad r t) (pad r t)

/-
A binary tree of height `h` has at most `2^h` terminal transcripts.
-/
theorem leaves_le_two_pow_height (t : ComparisonTree) :
    leaves t ≤ 2 ^ height t := by
      induction' t with l r ihl ihr;
      · decide +revert;
      · refine le_trans ( add_le_add ihl ihr ) ?_;
        simp +arith +decide [ ComparisonTree.height ];
        cases max_cases l.height r.height <;> simp_all +decide [ pow_add ];
        · linarith [ pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by decide : 1 ≤ 2 ) ‹_› ];
        · linarith [ pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by decide : 1 ≤ 2 ) ( by linarith : l.height ≤ r.height ) ]

/-
Padding adds an arbitrary number of comparisons to every execution.
-/
theorem height_pad (r : ℕ) (t : ComparisonTree) :
    height (pad r t) = r + height t := by
      induction' r with r ih generalizing t <;> simp_all +arith +decide;
      · rfl;
      · rw [ show pad ( r + 1 ) t = ComparisonTree.branch ( pad r t ) ( pad r t ) from rfl, ComparisonTree.height ] ; simp +arith +decide [ ih ]

/-
Padding never decreases the number of available transcripts.
-/
theorem leaves_le_pad (r : ℕ) (t : ComparisonTree) :
    leaves t ≤ leaves (pad r t) := by
      induction' r with r ih generalizing t;
      · rfl;
      · exact le_trans ( ih t ) ( by exact le_add_of_nonneg_left ( Nat.zero_le _ ) )

end ComparisonTree

/-- A comparison-tree shape can distinguish all orderings of `n` distinct items when it
has at least `n!` terminal transcripts. -/
def SortsOrderings (t : ComparisonTree) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n.factorial ≤ t.leaves

/-
**Exact information lower bound.** Every comparison tree capable of distinguishing
all `n!` orderings has worst-case height at least `⌈log₂(n!)⌉`.
-/
theorem comparison_lower_bound (t : ComparisonTree) (n : ℕ)
    (hs : SortsOrderings t n) :
    Nat.clog 2 n.factorial ≤ t.height := by
      exact Nat.le_trans ( Nat.clog_mono_right _ <| show n.factorial ≤ 2 ^ t.height from hs.trans <|ComparisonTree.leaves_le_two_pow_height t ) ( by norm_num )

/-
Redundant comparisons can increase worst-case comparison count arbitrarily while
preserving the ability to sort the same inputs.
-/
theorem redundant_comparisons_preserve_sorting (t : ComparisonTree) (n r : ℕ)
    (hs : SortsOrderings t n) :
    SortsOrderings (t.pad r) n ∧ (t.pad r).height = r + t.height := by
      exact ⟨ le_trans hs ( ComparisonTree.leaves_le_pad r t ), ComparisonTree.height_pad r t ⟩

/-- The information erased by the sorting map, for **every** `n`: the map is constant,
so the image is a single point and the erased information is `log₂ (n!)`.  (The imported
`sorting_info_erased` carries a `1 ≤ n` hypothesis that this computation does not need.) -/
theorem infoErased_sortingFunction (n : ℕ) :
    infoErased (sortingFunction n) = Real.logb 2 n.factorial := by
  classical
  have hne : (Finset.univ : Finset (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))).Nonempty := Finset.univ_nonempty
  unfold infoErased sortingFunction
  rw [Finset.image_const hne]
  simp [Fintype.card_perm]

/-
**Three-way factorial synthesis.** A correct comparison tree obeys the entropy lower
bound; irreversible sorting erases exactly `log₂(n!)` bits; and every reversible
implementation needs at least `n!` history states.
-/
theorem factorial_controls_comparisons_entropy_and_history
    (t : ComparisonTree) (n : ℕ) (hs : SortsOrderings t n)
    (Aux : Type*) [Fintype Aux]
    (e : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) ≃ Unit × Aux)
    (hc : ∀ σ, (e σ).1 = sortingFunction n σ) :
    Nat.clog 2 n.factorial ≤ t.height ∧
    infoErased (sortingFunction n) = Real.logb 2 n.factorial ∧
    n.factorial ≤ Fintype.card Aux := by
      refine' ⟨ comparison_lower_bound t n hs, _, _ ⟩;
      · exact infoErased_sortingFunction n
      · convert sorting_history_lower_bound n Aux e hc using 1;
        simp +decide [ Fintype.card_perm ]

/-
**Exact Landauer scale for sorting.** With natural logarithms, erasing the unknown
input permutation costs `kT · log(n!)`.  The factor `log 2` in the per-bit cost cancels
the change of base in `log₂(n!)`.
-/
theorem sorting_landauer_gap_exact (n : ℕ) (kT : ℝ) :
    landauerGap (sortingFunction n) kT = kT * Real.log n.factorial := by
      have h2 : Real.log 2 ≠ 0 := (Real.log_pos (by norm_num)).ne'

The Landauer work assigned to irreversible sorting is unchanged when redundant
comparison levels are inserted.  Consequently, comparison count alone cannot equal
logical-erasure work without an additional physical model for how comparisons are reset.
-/
theorem padding_changes_comparisons_not_landauer_work
    (t : ComparisonTree) (n r : ℕ) (hs : SortsOrderings t n) (kT : ℝ) :
    SortsOrderings (t.pad r) n ∧
    (t.pad r).height = r + t.height ∧
    landauerGap (sortingFunction n) kT = landauerGap (sortingFunction n) kT := by
      exact ⟨ redundant_comparisons_preserve_sorting t n r hs |>.1, redundant_comparisons_preserve_sorting t n r hs |>.2, rfl ⟩

-- reversible history, and thermodynamic erasure, while exposing the proposed law
-- “one comparison costs one bit” as too coarse.

-- Synthesis: The surviving claim is a three-way lower-bound principle.  Factorial entropy

-- on which information is eventually erased and on the physical implementation.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--

end SortingEntropyWork",

This file packages the results of `Asymptotics.lean` and `FiniteParity.lean` into the

> distinct asymptotic expansions according to the parity of the initial population, with a
> common leading limit but different first-order corrections.

* `n` even:  `villageWin (n - k) k = 1 - k·√(2/π)·n^{-1/2} + o(n^{-1/2})`,

`π/2`, independently of `k`.

* `parityCoeff` : the parity-dependent first-order coefficient `k·√(2/π)` / `k·√(π/2)`.
* `villageWin_expansion_even` / `villageWin_expansion_odd` : the two expansions, stated as
  convergence of the rescaled defect `√n · (1 - villageWin (n-k) k)`.
* `parityCoeff_ne` : for `k ≥ 1` the two first-order coefficients are different, so the two

* `parityCoeff_ratio` : their ratio is `π/2`, uniformly in `k`.
* `village_parity_dichotomy` : the full conjecture in one statement — common leading limit,
  distinct first-order coefficients with ratio `π/2`, and (consequently) no single
  parity-blind `n^{-1/2}` expansion.
* `village_parity_dichotomy_finite` : the non-asymptotic shadow of the dichotomy at

as a function of the wolf count `k` and the parity of the population
(`true` = even population, `false` = odd population). -/

  if even then (k : ℝ) * Real.sqrt (2 / π) else (k : ℝ) * Real.sqrt (π / 2)

theorem parityCoeff_even (k : ℕ) : parityCoeff k true = (k : ℝ) * Real.sqrt (2 / π) := rfl

theorem parityCoeff_odd (k : ℕ) : parityCoeff k false = (k : ℝ) * Real.sqrt (π / 2) := rfl

/-- **Even-population expansion.**  Along even populations `n = 2m`, the rescaled defect

  have h := tendsto_scaled_failProb_even_pop k

  rw [villageWin]
  push_cast
  ring

/-- **Odd-population expansion.**  Along odd populations `n = 2m+1`, the rescaled defect
converges instead to `k·√(π/2)`. -/
theorem villageWin_expansion_odd (k : ℕ) :
    Tendsto (fun m : ℕ =>
        Real.sqrt (2 * (m : ℝ) + 1) * (1 - ((villageWin (2 * m + 1 - k) k : ℚ) : ℝ))) atTop

# Cycle 4: the two shadows, and when a factor-local run actually reveals the factor

Cycles 1–3 showed that the cost of a natural method modulo `N = p·q` is carried by the
mod-`p` shadow alone.  What the shadow does *not* by itself decide is whether the run
**succeeds**: the gcd taken at a mod-`p` collision is a proper factor only if the same
pair of states does not also collide modulo `q`.  This file resolves that interaction
exactly, for arbitrary state sequences and hence for every uniform method.

* `zmod_eq_of_shadows_eq` — two states modulo `p·q` (coprime factors) are equal as soon
  as both shadows agree: CRT injectivity in the form needed here.
* `seqColl_iff_shadows` — **collision decomposition**: a sequence modulo `p·q` collides
  at time `n` iff both shadows collide at `n` *with a common witness index*.  This is
  the exact converse of the inequality `collTime_map_le` of cycle 2, and it explains why
  the modulus-level collision is generally strictly later than either shadow's.
* `shadow_collTime_le` — each shadow is never slower than the modulus run.
* `val_congr_of_shadow_eq` — a mod-`p` agreement of states is a congruence of their
  integer representatives.
* `reveal_of_shadow_strictly_earlier` — **the success criterion**: whenever the mod-`p`
  shadow collides strictly before the modulus run does, the gcd computed at that
  collision is a nontrivial proper divisor of `N` divisible by `p`.  Combined with
  `MethodLocalityNat.reveal_dichotomy` this closes the loop: factor-local cost *plus* a
  strictly earlier shadow equals a factor, deterministically.
* `success_criterion` — the synthesis for uniform methods.

namespace MethodLocalityCRT

open MethodLocality MethodLocalityNat

/-! ## 1. CRT: the two shadows determine the state -/

/-- Reduction to the first factor. -/
abbrev fstHom (p q : ℕ) : ZMod (p * q) →+* ZMod p := ZMod.castHom (Dvd.intro q rfl) (ZMod p)

/-- Reduction to the second factor. -/
abbrev sndHom (p q : ℕ) : ZMod (p * q) →+* ZMod q := ZMod.castHom (Dvd.intro_left p rfl) (ZMod q)

/-- **CRT injectivity.**  Agreement of both shadows is agreement of the states. -/
theorem zmod_eq_of_shadows_eq {p q : ℕ} (hco : Nat.Coprime p q) {x y : ZMod (p * q)}
    (hp : fstHom p q x = fstHom p q y) (hq : sndHom p q x = sndHom p q y) : x = y := by
  refine (ZMod.chineseRemainder hco).injective ?_
  ext
  · simpa [ZMod.chineseRemainder] using hp
  · simpa [ZMod.chineseRemainder] using hq

/-! ## 2. Collision decomposition -/

/-- **The modulus collides exactly when both shadows collide together.**  Note the
quantifier: a *common* witness index is required, which is why the modulus-level
collision time is in general strictly larger than both shadow times. -/
theorem seqColl_iff_shadows {p q : ℕ} (hco : Nat.Coprime p q) (s : ℕ → ZMod (p * q)) (n : ℕ) :
    SeqColl s n ↔ ∃ i < n, fstHom p q (s i) = fstHom p q (s n) ∧
      sndHom p q (s i) = sndHom p q (s n) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨i, hi, hEq⟩
    exact ⟨i, hi, by rw [hEq], by rw [hEq]⟩
  · rintro ⟨i, hi, h1, h2⟩
    exact ⟨i, hi, zmod_eq_of_shadows_eq hco h1 h2⟩

/-- Each shadow collides no later than the modulus run. -/
theorem shadow_collTime_le {p q : ℕ} [NeZero (p * q)] (s : ℕ → ZMod (p * q)) :
    collTime (fun n => fstHom p q (s n)) ≤ collTime s :=
  collTime_map_le _ _

/-! ## 3. From a shadow collision to a factor -/

/-- A mod-`p` agreement of two states modulo `N` is a congruence of their canonical
integer representatives. -/
theorem val_congr_of_shadow_eq {p N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (h : p ∣ N) {x y : ZMod N}

    x.val ≡ y.val [MOD p] := by

    intro z
    have hz : ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod N) = z := ZMod.natCast_rightInverse z
    calc (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) z
        = (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod N) := by rw [hz]
      _ = ((z.val : ℕ) : ZMod p) := map_natCast _ _
  rw [hcast x, hcast y] at hEq
  exact (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff _ _ _).mp hEq

distinct modulo `N`, and the gcd of their difference with `N` is a nontrivial proper
divisor of `N` that is a multiple of `p`: the factor is out. -/
theorem reveal_of_shadow_strictly_earlier {p N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (hp : 2 ≤ p) (h : p ∣ N)
    (s : ℕ → ZMod N)
    (hlt : collTime (fun n => (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (s n)) < collTime s) :
    ∃ d : ℕ, 0 < d ∧ d < N ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd d N ∧ Nat.gcd d N < N ∧ 2 ≤ Nat.gcd d N := by
  haveI : NeZero p := ⟨by omega⟩
  set t : ℕ → ZMod p := fun n => (ZMod.castHom h (ZMod p)) (s n) with ht
  obtain ⟨i, hi, hEq⟩ := collTime_mem t
  have hne : s i ≠ s (collTime t) := by
    intro hcontra
    exact not_seqColl_of_lt_collTime (s := s) hlt ⟨i, hi, hcontra⟩
  have hvne : (s i).val ≠ (s (collTime t)).val := fun hv => hne (ZMod.val_injective N hv)
  have hcong : (s i).val ≡ (s (collTime t)).val [MOD p] := val_congr_of_shadow_eq h hEq
  rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hvne with hlt' | hlt'
  · refine ⟨(s (collTime t)).val - (s i).val, by omega, by
      have := ZMod.val_lt (s (collTime t)); omega, ?_⟩
    obtain ⟨h1, -, h3, h4⟩ :=

    exact ⟨h1, h3, h4⟩
  · refine ⟨(s i).val - (s (collTime t)).val, by omega, by
      have := ZMod.val_lt (s i); omega, ?_⟩
    obtain ⟨h1, -, h3, h4⟩ := factor_revealed hp h hlt' (ZMod.val_lt (s i)) hcong

natural state update, if the factor's shadow closes before the modulus run does, the
run outputs a nontrivial proper factor of `N` divisible by `p`. -/
theorem success_criterion (M : UniformStep) {p N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (hp : 2 ≤ p) (h : p ∣ N)
    (x0 : ℤ)
    (hlt : uniformTime M p N h x0 < collTime (M.orbit (ZMod N) ((x0 : ZMod N)))) :
    ∃ d : ℕ, 0 < d ∧ d < N ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd d N ∧ Nat.gcd d N < N ∧ 2 ≤ Nat.gcd d N :=

/-!
# The sharp union-bound defect: `n · defect ≤ k(k-1)/2`

`Bounds.lean` proves the union bound `failProb v k ≤ k · surv (v+k)` together with an
*existential* `O(1/n)` reverse bound.  This file replaces the existential constant by the
explicit value `k(k-1)/2 = C(k,2)` — the number of unordered pairs of wolves — and shows
that this constant is **optimal**: it is attained exactly, at every odd population, for
`k = 2` and `k = 3`.

The engine is the exact *defect recursion*

`(v+k+3) · defect (v+2) (k+1) = (k+1) · defect (v+1) k + (v+2) · defect v (k+1)`,

in which the union-bound term `k · surv n` cancels identically because `surv` satisfies the
same one-step ladder as the population.  Writing `g v k = (v+k)·defect v k`, this becomes

`g (v+2) (k+1) = [ (k+1)·g (v+1) k + (v+2)·g v (k+1) ] / (v+k+1)`,

a convex-combination-like recursion for which `C(k,2)` is a *fixed point*: substituting
`g(v+1,k) = C(k,2)` and `g(v,k+1) = C(k+1,2)` on the right reproduces `C(k+1,2)` exactly.
That is the structural reason the constant is `C(k,2)` and not something else.

## Main results

* `surv_le_surv_add_two`, `surv_add_six_le_half` : elementary monotonicity of the survival
  ladder along a fixed parity, and the numerical bound `surv n ≤ 1/2` for `n ≥ 6`.
* `mul_surv_le_half` : `k · surv k ≤ (k+1)/2`.
* `surv_sq_odd_le`, `mul_surv_sq_le_two` : a purely rational proof that `n · surv n ^ 2 ≤ 2`
  — an elementary bound on the Wallis product, with no analysis.
* `defect_recursion` : the exact defect recursion.
* `defect_scaled_le` : **the sharp bound** `(v+k) · defect v k ≤ k(k-1)/2`.
* `failProb_ge_sharp` : the resulting explicit two-sided estimate for the wolf-win
  probability.
* `sharp_constant_attained_two_wolves`, `sharp_constant_attained_three_wolves` :
  optimality of the constant `C(k,2)` for `k = 2, 3`.
